events.title: Rome declares war; the Carthaginian surrender and the final demand
events.summary: Rome declared war on Carthage. Utica had already surrendered to Rome. Carthage too made a formal deditio, handing over 300 children of noble families as hostages and then, at the consuls' demand, 200,000 sets of armour and 2,000 catapults. Only then did the consuls Manius Manilius and Lucius Marcius Censorinus announce the Senate's final condition: the Carthaginians must abandon their city and resettle at least 80 stades (about 15 km) from the sea. Carthage refused and prepared to fight.
events.detail: In desperation the Carthaginians freed slaves, worked day and night in the temples making weapons, and, the tradition says, cut off women's hair for catapult cords. Polybius (36.2-9) records the debate among Greeks over whether Rome had acted justly; Appian (Libyca 74-93) preserves Censorinus' speech arguing that a city by the sea breeds dangerous ambitions.
scholarship: Harris, War and Imperialism in Republican Rome (1979)
Astin, Scipio Aemilianus (1967)
Miles, Carthage Must Be Destroyed (2010)
events.debate: Polybius 36.9 reports four Greek views on the morality of Rome's conduct. Modern debate pits Roman fear and Catonian ideology against greed for land and plunder and the desire to forestall Masinissa.

events.title: Lex Calpurnia de repetundis: the first permanent criminal court
events.summary: The tribune Lucius Calpurnius Piso Frugi carried a law creating a standing court (quaestio perpetua) under a praetor, with a jury of senators, to hear claims by provincials and allies for the recovery of money illegally taken by Roman magistrates (pecuniae repetundae).
events.detail: Cicero (Brutus 106) calls it the first such law. Its procedure was civil rather than penal: restitution, not punishment. It became the model for the system of standing criminal courts that Gaius Gracchus (who transferred juries to the equites), Sulla and Augustus developed, and the control of the repetundae juries became one of the great political battlegrounds of the late Republic.
scholarship: Lintott, Judicial Reform and Land Reform in the Roman Republic (1992)
Richardson, 'The Purpose of the Lex Calpurnia de repetundis', JRS 77 (1987)
events.debate: J. S. Richardson argued that the law served Roman interests in controlling governors more than provincial redress.

events.title: Death of Cato the Elder
events.summary: Cato died at about 85, in the year the war he had demanded began. In his last months he spoke against Galba and was still writing the Origines, the first history of Rome in Latin prose, which omitted the names of generals and recorded the deeds of the Roman people as a whole (and the name of a brave Carthaginian elephant, Surus).

events.title: Siege of Carthage
events.summary: For three years Rome besieged Carthage, a city of perhaps 200,000 behind a triple wall across the isthmus. The consuls of 149 failed: Censorinus breached the wall but was repulsed, and his fleet was burned by fireships. Only the military tribune Scipio Aemilianus distinguished himself. In 147 Aemilianus, now consul, cut the city off by land and built a great mole across the harbour mouth; the Carthaginians dug a new channel and sailed out a fleet built in secret, but delayed and lost the chance. In spring 146 Laelius stormed the Cothon and the Romans fought for six days from house to house up the streets to the Byrsa.
events.detail: Appian (Libyca 94-135), based on Polybius, who was present, is the main account. Excavations have revealed the circular naval harbour with ship sheds for some 170 ships and the 'Quartier Hannibal' on the Byrsa slope, destroyed in 146 and buried under Roman terracing.

sides.strength: c. 80,000 in 149 (Appian; probably exaggerated), later c. 40,000
citizens, freed slaves and field army

battle.significance: Ended Carthage as a state after some 670 years.

scholarship: Astin, Scipio Aemilianus (1967)
Lancel, Carthage (1992)
Hurst, Excavations at Carthage: The British Mission II.1, The Circular Harbour, North Side (1994)

events.title: Andriscus, the false Philip
events.summary: Andriscus, a man of humble origin from Adramyttium who claimed to be Philip, son of Perseus, escaped from Roman custody, raised Thracian support and was proclaimed king in Macedonia, reuniting the four republics. In 148 he defeated and killed the praetor Publius Juventius Thalna and briefly controlled Thessaly.

events.title: Second battle of Pydna
events.summary: The praetor Quintus Caecilius Metellus, supported by the fleet of Attalus II, defeated Andriscus near Pydna. Andriscus fled to Thrace, where the chief Byzes handed him over. Metellus took the cognomen Macedonicus. Macedonia was thereafter governed directly as a Roman province.

battle.significance: Ended Macedonian independence for good; led to the province of Macedonia.

events.title: Viriathus' victory at Tribola
events.summary: Viriathus, chosen leader by Lusitanians surrounded by the praetor Gaius Vetilius, ordered his men to scatter and later regroup while he held off the Romans with a thousand horsemen. He then lured Vetilius' army into an ambush in thickets near Tribola. Vetilius was captured and killed by a Lusitanian who thought the fat old man not worth ransoming; 6,000 of his 10,000 men escaped.

battle.significance: Launched Viriathus' eight-year career of victories.

events.title: Scipio Aemilianus elected consul under age
events.summary: Scipio Aemilianus, aged about 37 and standing only for the aedileship, was demanded as consul by a popular movement frustrated with the failures at Carthage. The presiding consul cited the Lex Villia; the tribunes threatened to take the elections from the consuls; the Senate had the law suspended for a year. The people also assigned him Africa by vote instead of the lot.
events.detail: The episode set a precedent for popular intervention in the allocation of commands, exploited later by Marius and others.
scholarship: Astin, Scipio Aemilianus (1967)

events.title: Capture of Nepheris
events.summary: In winter 147/146 Scipio Aemilianus sent Laelius and Gulussa to destroy the Carthaginian field army under Diogenes at Nepheris, the base that supplied the besieged city. Appian claims 70,000 killed, including non-combatants, and 10,000 captured. Nepheris fell after a 22-day siege.

sides.strength: Roman troops and Numidians under Gulussa

events.title: Destruction of Carthage
events.summary: After six days of street fighting, 50,000 men, women and children came down from the Byrsa and were spared to be sold. Some 900 Roman deserters burned themselves in the temple of Eshmun. Hasdrubal surrendered and knelt before Scipio; his wife, cursing him, killed their children and threw herself into the flames. The city burned for days. Watching it, Scipio wept and quoted Homer's lines on the fall of Troy, saying to Polybius that he feared the same fate would one day befall Rome.
events.detail: A Senate commission of ten ordered the city razed, cursed the site, and made its territory Roman public land. Before the assault, according to Macrobius (3.9), Scipio performed an evocatio inviting the tutelary deity of Carthage to come to Rome. The story that the Romans sowed salt in the ruins is a modern invention, first found in the 19th century (Ridley). Carthage was refounded as a Roman colony by Caesar and Augustus.
scholarship: Ridley, 'To Be Taken with a Pinch of Salt: The Destruction of Carthage', CPh 81 (1986)
Astin, Scipio Aemilianus (1967)
events.debate: The salting of Carthage is a myth; the curse on the site is attested. Sallust and others dated the moral decline of Rome to the removal of the Carthaginian threat (metus Punicus) in this year.

events.title: Creation of the province of Africa
events.summary: Carthage's territory became the province of Africa, governed from Utica, which with six other towns that had sided with Rome (Hadrumetum, Leptis Minor, Thapsus, Achulla, Usalis and Teudalis) became a free city. The boundary with Numidia was marked by a ditch, the fossa regia. Carthage's libraries were given to the Numidian kings, except Mago's 28 books on agriculture, which the Senate had translated into Latin.
events.detail: Mago's treatise, translated under the direction of Decimus Junius Silanus, became the foundation of Roman agronomy and was cited by Varro, Columella and Pliny.

sources.r: CIL I² 585 = Crawford, Roman Statutes no. 2

events.title: Battle of Scarpheia
events.summary: The Achaean League, under its strategos Critolaus, rejected Roman demands to detach Sparta, Corinth, Argos and other cities and declared war, nominally on Sparta. Quintus Caecilius Metellus marched south from Macedonia and caught the Achaean army at Scarpheia in Locris; Critolaus disappeared in the rout, perhaps drowned in the marshes or by poison.
events.detail: Polybius, whose account survives in fragments (38.9-18), blamed the Achaean leaders' demagoguery and the masses' folly, a judgement shaped by his own position as friend of Rome.

sides.losses: heavy; 1,000 Arcadians later destroyed at Chaeronea

events.debate: Polybius' hostility to Critolaus and Diaeus colours the tradition; Pausanias says Critolaus was never found.

events.title: Battle of Corinth (Leucopetra)
events.summary: The consul Lucius Mummius, with 23,000 foot and 3,500 horse, defeated the last Achaean army under Diaeus, reinforced by 12,000 freed and armed slaves, on the Isthmus at Leucopetra. Diaeus fled to Megalopolis, killed his wife and poisoned himself.

sides.strength: 23,000 foot, 3,500 horse plus Cretan archers and Pergamenes (Pausanias)

events.title: Sack of Corinth
events.summary: Mummius entered Corinth, killed the men, sold the women and children into slavery and, on the Senate's orders, razed the city. Its art treasures were shipped to Rome and distributed to Italian towns. Polybius, who was present, saw soldiers playing dice on famous paintings thrown on the ground, among them Aristides' Dionysus.
events.detail: Mummius, a 'new man', became a byword for philistinism: Velleius (1.13.4) says he warned the shippers that if they lost any of the paintings and statues they would have to replace them with new ones. The Achaean League was dissolved and Greece placed under the supervision of the governor of Macedonia; Polybius helped the commissioners frame new constitutions and was honoured with statues across the Peloponnese. Corinth lay in ruins until Caesar's colony of 44.
events.debate: Archaeology shows some continued occupation at Corinth after 146, so the destruction was not total. Pliny's story that 'Corinthian bronze' was an alloy formed when the city burned is fanciful.

events.title: Province of Macedonia and the Via Egnatia
events.summary: After Andriscus, Macedonia became a permanent Roman province, with responsibility for supervising Greece and defending the northern frontier against Thracians and Scordisci. Within a few years the proconsul Gnaeus Egnatius built the Via Egnatia from Dyrrachium and Apollonia across the Balkans to Thessalonica, later extended to the Hebrus and Byzantium.
events.detail: A bilingual milestone of Egnatius found near Thessalonica and published in 1974 dates the road to c. 145-120. The province's era was reckoned from 148.

sources.w: Bilingual milestone of Cn. Egnatius near Thessalonica

events.debate: Whether the province dates from 148 or 146, and the exact date of the road, are debated.

events.title: Temple of Jupiter Stator: the first marble temple in Rome
events.summary: Quintus Caecilius Metellus Macedonicus built a temple of Jupiter Stator, designed by the Greek architect Hermodorus of Salamis and the first temple in Rome built entirely of marble, beside a rebuilt temple of Juno Regina, within a new colonnade, the Porticus Metelli. In front he set Lysippus' bronze group of the 25 Companions of Alexander who fell at the Granicus, taken from Dion in Macedonia.
events.debate: Construction may have begun after Metellus' triumph of 146 and finished somewhat later.

events.title: Triumph of Mummius 'Achaicus'
events.summary: Lucius Mummius triumphed over Achaea and Corinth, taking the cognomen Achaicus, the first new man to earn a victory title. He dedicated a temple to Hercules Victor, whose dedicatory inscription survives, and distributed Corinthian statues to towns in Italy and as far as Spain, many with his name inscribed.
events.detail: The surviving dedication (CIL I² 626) reads that Achaea was captured and Corinth destroyed under his leadership and auspices. Inscribed bases of Mummian dedications have been found at Italica, Parma, Nursia and elsewhere.

sources.w: Dedication of L. Mummius to Hercules Victor

events.title: Construction of the Aqua Marcia
events.summary: The praetor Quintus Marcius Rex was given 180 million sesterces to repair the old aqueducts and build a new one, the Aqua Marcia, bringing cold, clear water some 91 km from the upper Anio valley, the last 10 km on high arches. When the decemvirs found a Sibylline objection to bringing water to the Capitol, the Senate overrode it.
events.detail: Frontinus (De aquis 1.7) gives the figures. The Marcia was the longest and most admired of Rome's aqueducts, and its water was considered the best; Pliny calls it the most famous water in the world.
events.locName: Rome, from the upper Anio valley

events.title: Appius Claudius' triumph and his Vestal daughter
events.summary: Denied a triumph over the Alpine Salassi, the consul Appius Claudius Pulcher triumphed at his own expense. When a tribune tried to drag him from the chariot, his daughter Claudia, a Vestal Virgin, climbed in beside him; the tribune dared not touch her, and the procession reached the Capitol.

events.title: Censorship of Scipio Aemilianus
events.summary: As censor with the lenient Lucius Mummius, Scipio Aemilianus took a severe line on morals. At the closing lustrum he reportedly changed the traditional prayer asking the gods to make the Roman state better and greater, saying it was great and good enough, and asked them instead to preserve it for ever. The arches of the Pons Aemilius were completed.
events.debate: The prayer story may be a later invention reflecting the 'limits of empire' theme.

events.title: Erisane: Servilianus capitulates to Viriathus
events.summary: While Quintus Fabius Maximus Servilianus besieged Erisane, Viriathus slipped into the town by night, attacked the Roman siege lines and drove the army into a gorge where it was trapped. Viriathus let the Romans go on terms: peace, recognition of the Lusitanians' land, and Viriathus' status as a friend of the Roman people. The Roman people ratified the treaty.
events.detail: Within months the next governor, Quintus Servilius Caepio, persuaded the Senate to let him renew the war.

battle.significance: The high point of Viriathus' career: Rome recognised him as amicus populi Romani.

events.title: Lex Gabinia tabellaria: the secret ballot
events.summary: The tribune Aulus Gabinius carried a law introducing the secret written ballot (tabella) in elections, replacing oral voting announced to officials. It was followed by the Lex Cassia (137) for trials before the people, the Lex Papiria (131) for legislation and the Lex Coelia (107) for treason trials.
events.detail: Cicero (De legibus 3.35) regarded the ballot laws as destroying the authority of the optimates over voters. They reduced aristocratic control of the clientele and helped make the populares politics of the Gracchi possible.
scholarship: Yakobson, 'Secret Ballot and its Effects in the Late Roman Republic', Hermes 123 (1995)

events.title: Astrologers and Jews expelled from Rome
events.summary: The praetor peregrinus Gnaeus Cornelius Hispalus ordered the Chaldaean astrologers to leave Rome and Italy within ten days, and also expelled Jews who, the epitome says, tried to corrupt Roman morals with the cult of 'Jupiter Sabazius', and removed their private altars.
events.detail: The passage survives only in two epitomes of Valerius Maximus (1.3.3); the reference to Sabazius may be a confusion with the Jewish divine title Sabaoth. It is the earliest notice of Jews in Rome.
events.debate: Whether the expelled were Jews, worshippers of the Phrygian Sabazius or both is debated.

events.title: Murder of Viriathus
events.summary: Quintus Servilius Caepio bribed three of Viriathus' envoys, Audax, Ditalcus and Minurus, who stabbed him in the throat as he slept in his armour. The Lusitanians burned him on a great pyre and held funeral games with 200 pairs of fighters at his tomb. When the assassins came for their reward, later tradition says, they were told Rome did not approve of soldiers killing their general.
events.detail: Viriathus' career made him a hero of Iberian and Portuguese national memory. His successor Tautalus soon surrendered, and Decimus Junius Brutus settled the Lusitanian veterans at Valentia (138).
events.debate: The phrase usually quoted ('Rome does not pay traitors') is not ancient in that form; the refusal of reward is reported by Eutropius and Orosius.

events.title: Tribunes imprison the consuls over the levy
events.summary: The tribune Gaius Curiatius, angered by the consuls' refusal to grant exemptions from service in Spain, had the consuls Decimus Junius Brutus and Publius Cornelius Scipio Nasica thrown into prison. Curiatius gave Nasica the mocking nickname Serapio, after a sacrificial attendant he resembled. Grain prices and the levy were becoming flashpoints of popular politics.

events.title: Foundation of Valentia
events.summary: Decimus Junius Brutus gave land and a town, Valentia, to those who had fought under Viriathus. Excavations at L'Almoina in Valencia have found the earliest Roman buildings and a foundation-period deposit consistent with that date.

events.title: Brutus Callaicus crosses the River of Forgetfulness
events.summary: Decimus Junius Brutus campaigned north through Lusitania into Gallaecia, crossing the Durius (Douro). At the Limia, which local belief held to be the Lethe, river of forgetfulness, his soldiers refused to cross; Brutus seized a standard, crossed, and called each man by name from the far bank. He reached the Minius and, Florus says, saw the sun sink into the Ocean. He took the cognomen Callaicus.

events.title: Surrender of Mancinus at Numantia
events.summary: The consul Gaius Hostilius Mancinus, panicked by a false rumour of approaching Cantabri and Vaccaei, abandoned his camp near Numantia at night and was trapped with 20,000 men. The Numantines would only negotiate with his quaestor, Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus, whose father they trusted. The treaty saved the army, recognised Numantine independence, and was sworn by Mancinus and his officers.
events.detail: The Senate repudiated the treaty. Plutarch (Tiberius Gracchus 5-7) argues that the humiliation of seeing his treaty disowned set Tiberius against the Senate leadership, a contributing cause of the crisis of 133.

battle.significance: The low point of Roman arms in Spain; the repudiated treaty radicalised Tiberius Gracchus.

events.title: Lex Cassia tabellaria
events.summary: The tribune Lucius Cassius Longinus Ravilla extended the secret ballot to trials before the popular assemblies, except cases of treason (perduellio).

events.title: Mancinus handed over to the Numantines
events.summary: To free Rome from the oath of the repudiated treaty, the Senate decreed that Mancinus be surrendered to the Numantines. The fetial priests delivered him naked and bound before the town gate; the Numantines refused to accept him, saying that the guilt for broken faith could not be shifted onto one man. After a day he was taken back, later had a statue of himself made showing him in that state, and even resumed a public career.
events.detail: The case was debated by jurists for centuries: whether a man surrendered and refused had lost his citizenship (postliminium).

events.title: Outbreak of the First Servile War
events.summary: In Sicily, where great estates were worked by masses of slaves, many recently enslaved in Rome's wars, slaves of the cruel Damophilus of Enna rose under Eunus, a Syrian slave and prophet who breathed fire by hiding a nutshell of burning sulphur in his mouth. They took Enna, massacred their masters and proclaimed Eunus king under the name Antiochus. Cleon, a Cilician herdsman, raised the slaves of the Agrigentum region and joined him.
events.detail: Diodorus (34/35.2), deriving from Posidonius, is the main source, in Byzantine excerpts. Eunus struck bronze coins inscribed BA ANTIO with Demeter and an ear of grain. Numbers are uncertain: Livy's epitome gives 70,000 rebels, Diodorus 200,000. Several praetors and consuls were defeated.
scholarship: Bradley, Slavery and Rebellion in the Roman World, 140 B.C.-70 B.C. (1989)
Shaw, Spartacus and the Slave Wars (2001)
events.debate: The start date (136 or 135, or even 140s) is uncertain; Diodorus' figures are inflated; how far the revolt aimed at a Hellenistic-style kingdom rather than abolition of slavery is debated.

events.title: Siege of Numantia
events.summary: Elected consul for 134 by special exemption from the law against second consulships, Scipio Aemilianus restored discipline to the demoralised army in Spain, expelling 2,000 prostitutes and the traders, and then encircled Numantia with a continuous wall about 9 km long, linking seven camps and towers, with the Duero blocked by booms of spiked timbers. Some 60,000 men, including Numidians under the young Jugurtha, besieged 4,000-8,000 Numantines. After fifteen months of starvation and cannibalism the city surrendered in summer 133; many inhabitants killed themselves. Scipio kept fifty for his triumph, sold the rest and razed the town.
events.detail: Appian (Iberica 84-98), from Polybius, who was present, is the main narrative. The Numantine Rhetogenes broke out with five friends to seek help from Lutia, whose young men wanted to come; Scipio cut off the right hands of 400 of them. Adolf Schulten's excavations (1905-1912) uncovered the Roman camps and circumvallation, the most complete Roman siege works of the Republic before Alesia. Gaius Marius, Jugurtha, the satirist Lucilius and the historian Sempronius Asellio served in the army. Scipio took the cognomen Numantinus and triumphed in 132.
events.locName: Numantia (Cerro de la Muela, Garray, Soria)

battle.significance: Ended the Celtiberian wars; Numantia became the symbol of Iberian resistance.

scholarship: Schulten, Numantia: Die Ergebnisse der Ausgrabungen 1905-1912 (1914-1931)
Astin, Scipio Aemilianus (1967)
Dobson, The Army of the Roman Republic: The Second Century BC, Polybius and the Camps at Numantia (2008)
events.debate: Dobson's re-examination of Schulten's camps questions some of Schulten's camp plans and dates. Figures for the defenders vary widely.

events.title: Attalus III bequeaths Pergamon to Rome
events.summary: Attalus III of Pergamon, the last of his dynasty, died in spring 133 leaving a will that bequeathed his kingdom to the Roman people, while the city of Pergamon itself was to be free. When the will reached Rome, Tiberius Gracchus proposed that the royal treasure be used to equip the new smallholders of his land law and that the people, not the Senate, decide on the cities of the kingdom.
events.detail: A Pergamene decree (OGIS 338) issued soon after the king's death confirms the will and extends citizenship to various groups to secure the city against the rising of Aristonicus, an illegitimate son of Eumenes II who claimed the throne as Eumenes III and rallied the poor and slaves as 'Heliopolitans', with the Stoic Blossius of Cumae as adviser. The war lasted until 129, when Manius Aquillius organised the province of Asia, which became the richest source of Roman revenue.

sources.w: Pergamene decree on the will of Attalus III

scholarship: Kallet-Marx, Hegemony to Empire: The Development of the Roman Imperium in the East from 148 to 62 B.C. (1995)
Sherwin-White, Roman Foreign Policy in the East (1984)
events.debate: Why Attalus made the bequest (fear of social revolution, ensuring the cities' freedom, or Roman pressure) is unknown. Some modern scholars doubt Attalus' reputation for eccentricity (gardening in poisonous plants, studying sculpture), which comes from hostile sources.

events.title: Rupilius ends the Sicilian slave war
events.summary: The consul Publius Rupilius starved out the rebel stronghold of Tauromenium, where the defenders were reduced to eating their children, and then took Enna through betrayal; Cleon fell fighting. Eunus fled with his bodyguard and was found hiding in a cave; he died in prison at Morgantina. Over 20,000 rebels were crucified or killed. Rupilius then drew up a charter for the province, the Lex Rupilia.
events.detail: Lead sling bullets inscribed with the name of Lucius Calpurnius Piso, consul of 133, have been found at Enna, documenting the earlier Roman siege attempts.

battle.significance: Ended the First Servile War; Sicilian agriculture was reorganised under the Lex Rupilia.

scholarship: Bradley, Slavery and Rebellion in the Roman World (1989)
